Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise' is not clinically coherent with the rest of the profile. The threat items center on hypervigilance about nighttime intrusion and safety checking in the home, while the memory and appraisal items focus on intrusive assault memories, danger, and physical vulnerability. Exercise avoidance addresses a different symptom domain and lacks plausible linkage to the selected threat, memory, or appraisal content. In contrast, magical thinking and mirror checking fit better with maladaptive attempts to manage threat and distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: These two selected items are difficult to reconcile within the same profile. A strong appraisal of permanent bodily damage implies acknowledgment of serious ongoing physical consequences, whereas telling oneself the event did not really happen or was not that bad reflects minimization/denial of the trauma's reality or impact. While some ambivalence can occur clinically, this pair pulls in opposing directions strongly enough to question internal coherence in this profile.

vignette:
Amara's Story

Amara was seventy-eight when the man came through her back door. It was a Tuesday evening in March, nearly two years ago now, and she had been in her studio—a converted garage behind the house she and her late husband Samuel had owned for forty-three years—finishing a series of bowls for a gallery show in Atlanta. The light was fading. She had not heard him force the lock; she heard only his footsteps on the concrete floor, and by the time she turned from the wheel, he was already there, his face obscured, his hand raised with something that caught what remained of the daylight. She was certain it was a knife. The memory of his presence came back to her now in images—the blur of his jacket, the particular angle of his arm, the way the studio suddenly felt too small—and when the memory arrived unbidden, which it did at least three times daily, it came with the sensation that it was happening again, that she was still standing at that wheel with her hands wet and her heart hammering so violently she thought it would break through her ribs.

He took her purse. He took Samuel's watch from the kitchen counter—the one she still had not been able to put away. He did not strike her, though she had braced for it, and when he left through the same door he had entered, Amara had stood motionless in the studio for a time she could not afterward account for. The police came. They found nothing that led anywhere. What he had taken was replaceable. What he had left behind was not.

In the weeks that followed, Amara had begun checking the locks. First, the back door lock—the one he had broken—which she now secured with a deadbolt and a chain and a wooden dowel wedged through the frame. Then the front door. Then the windows, each one, a ritual that now took her nearly forty minutes every evening before she could sit down. But sitting down brought no rest. Her body remained vigilant even when her mind knew, abstractly, that the doors were locked and the windows were latched. She would lie in bed at two or three in the morning, jolting awake with the conviction that someone was moving through the house, and she would rise and walk through the rooms, turning on lights, checking locks again, listening for the particular creak that might mean an intruder. She had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion maintained only through exhausting vigilance, and that her own body—her racing heart, her shallow breath, the trembling in her hands—was a traitor that could not be trusted or controlled.

The studio had become impossible. She had tried to return to her wheel in May, thinking that the familiar rhythm of clay might settle something in her, but the moment she was alone in that space with the door behind her, her mind filled with the image of his footsteps crossing the concrete. She found herself unable to concentrate, unable to feel the clay respond to her hands the way it once had. By July, she had stopped going in altogether. The gallery in Atlanta had to cancel her show. A collector who had commissioned a large installation piece had asked, after months of silence, if she was still working. She was not. The studio gathered dust. The wheel sat idle.

Her daughter, who lived in Charlotte, had noticed during a phone call in September that her mother's voice sounded thin, exhausted. When she visited, she found Amara thinner as well, and the house immaculate in a way that suggested obsession rather than care. Amara was checking mirrors constantly now—a habit she had developed because she could not shake the feeling that someone was behind her, that she needed to verify repeatedly that she was alone. She would stand in the hallway looking at her own face in the mirror above the dresser, reassuring herself, though the reassurance never held.

It was her daughter who finally insisted that Amara see someone, who said that what had happened to her mother two years ago was not something she should have to carry alone. Amara had resisted, believing that if she thought about the event directly, if she let herself fully acknowledge what had occurred, she would shatter. But the alternative—the endless checking, the sleepless nights, the abandonment of the work that had defined her life for sixty years—had become unbearable. She had called a therapist last week. She was terrified of what might happen if she began to speak about that Tuesday in March, but she was more terrified of living the rest of her life as a prisoner in her own home.
